title: Wormhole Geometry from a Magnetic Vortex
authors: Dušan Đorđ ević, Fabián Molina, Vladimir Juričić
abstract: Strong coupling to a magnetic texture makes an electron propagate through an emergent curved space. We show that an elementary vortex realizes the exterior spatial geometry of an Ellis wormhole: an ultrastatic throat with radius fixed by the topological charge and Hund exchange, cut off at short distances by the microscopic core. Two separable signatures follow directly: the electron deflection collapses onto a single Ellis curve governed by the vortex winding and exchange coupling, while the spin Berry phase produces a half-flux Aharonov--Bohm response switched on and off by winding parity. The same metric can be emulated in a designer honeycomb lattice, where the valley-symmetrized wave-packet response follows the predicted exterior geodesic. These signatures are accessible through real-space electron deflection and scattering, providing experimentally distinct probes of the emergent geometry and Berry flux. The magnetic vortex thus turns a topological defect into a tunable curved-space lens for electrons in quantum materials and designer lattices.
summary: This work demonstrates that the topological structure of a magnetic vortex induces an emergent curved space metric analogous to the exterior of an Ellis wormhole for electrons. The key findings are two experimentally distinct signatures: measurable electron deflection governed by the vortex winding, and a quantized Berry phase response dependent on winding parity. This establishes a powerful 'texture–geometry dictionary' applicable to quantum materials.
main_problem: The study investigates how the topology of a magnetic vortex dictates the effective geometry experienced by itinerant electrons, linking defects to curved spacetime analogues.
main_result: A single magnetic vortex defect successfully generates an emergent metric realizing the exterior spatial geometry of an Ellis wormhole. This effect is characterized by two distinct, measurable signatures: electron deflection and a half-flux Aharonov-Bohm response.
method: The analysis combines deriving effective metrics from spin textures with solving geodesic equations and performing partial-wave scattering analyses to quantify quantum phase shifts.
model_or_system: The system models electrons propagating in a background coupled strongly to an elementary magnetic vortex. The geometry is mathematically compared to the exterior of an Ellis wormhole, and the results are tested by emulating the metric in designer honeycomb lattices.
key_observables: Electron deflection angle ($\Theta(b)$), Berry phase flux (Aharonov-Bohm response), and the effective curved space metric ($ds^2$).
important_parameters: Vortex winding number ($q$), Hund exchange coupling ($J$), and the characteristic Ellis length scale ($a_q \propto q/\sqrt{J}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis focuses on the exterior, core-truncated region of the wormhole geometry; lattice simulations require valley symmetrization to isolate the metric response.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate vortex textures and corresponding geodesics showing negative Ricci curvature. Other figures demonstrate universal scaling laws for deflection angles ($\Theta \propto q^2/J$) and show engineered hoppings reproducing continuum geodesic profiles in lattices.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from deriving the effective metric from spin texture variations, calculating observable quantities like deflection via elliptic integrals, establishing two independent signatures (metric vs. Berry flux), and finally validating these predictions by simulating wave-packet propagation on artificial honeycomb lattices.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, physical mechanism—a magnetic vortex—to generate an effective curved spacetime geometry that can be probed using standard quantum scattering techniques in condensed matter systems.
